Airgorah A WiFi security auditing software Installation | Usage | Credits Airgorah is a WiFi security auditing software that can capture nearby WiFi traffic, discover clients connected to access points, perform deauthentication attacks, capture handshakes and PMKIDs, and crack the password of access points. It is written in Rust and uses GTK4 for the graphical part. ⭐ Don't forget to put a star if you like the project! Legal ⚠️ Airgorah is designed to be used in testing and discovering flaws in networks you are owner of. Performing attacks on WiFi networks you are not owner of is illegal in almost all countries. I am not responsible for whatever damage you may cause by using this software. Requirements This software only works on linux . The graphical interface runs as a normal
user (so it works under both X11 and Wayland ). When a privileged operation is
needed, it launches a small privileged agent ( airgorah-agent ) via polkit ,
which will prompt for authentication once. You will also need a wireless network card that supports monitor mode and packet injection . Installation The installation instructions are available here . Usage The documentation about the usage of the application is available here . License This project is released under MIT license. Contributing If you have any question about the usage of the application, do not hesitate to open a discussion If you want to report a bug or provide a feature, do not hesitate to open an issue or submit a pull request

Anthropic Cybersecurity Skills The largest open-source cybersecurity skills library for AI agents 818 production-grade cybersecurity skills · 34 security domains · 6 framework mappings · 26+ AI platforms Get Started · What's Inside · Frameworks · Platforms · Contributing ⚠️ Community Project — This is an independent, community-created project. Not affiliated with Anthropic PBC. 🔐 Authorized & lawful use only. This library includes offensive and dual-use techniques (e.g. red-team C2, phishing simulation, exploitation) intended for authorized penetration testing, security research, defense, and education . Only use them against systems you own or have explicit written permission to test, and comply with all applicable laws and rules of engagement. You are solely responsible for how you use these skills. See SECURITY.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . Give any AI agent the security skills of a senior analyst A junior analyst knows which Volatility3 plugin to run on a suspicious memory dump, which Sigma rules catch Kerberoasting, and how to scope a cloud breach across three providers. Your AI agent doesn't — unless you give it these skills. This repo contains 818 structured cybersecurity skills spanning 34 security domains , each following the agentskills.io open standard.  The library maps across six industry frameworks — MITRE ATT&CK, NIST CSF 2.0, MITRE ATLAS, MITRE D3FEND, NIST AI RMF, and the MITRE Fight Fraud Framework (F3) — with each skill mapped to the frameworks relevant to its type (a forensics skill carries ATT&CK + CSF; an AI-security skill adds ATLAS and AI RMF).  Clone it, point your agent at it, and your next security investigation gets expert-level guidance in seconds. Six frameworks, one skill library Each skill maps to the frameworks that fit its subject — ATT&CK and NIST CSF are near-universal, while ATLAS, AI RMF, D3FEND, and F3 apply where they're relevant. Framework coverage across the 817 skills: MITRE ATT&CK 805 · NIST CSF 2.0 804 · MITRE D3FEND 139 · NIST AI RMF 97 · MITRE F3 94 · MITRE ATLAS 93 . Framework Version Framework scope What it maps MITRE ATT&CK v19.1 15 tactics · Enterprise/Mobile/ICS Adversary behaviors and TTPs NIST CSF 2.0 2.0 6 functions · 22 categories · 106 subcategories Organizational security posture MITRE ATLAS 2026.07 101 techniques · 77 sub-techniques AI/ML adversarial threats MITRE D3FEND v1.4.0 270 techniques Defensive countermeasures NIST AI RMF 1.0 4 functions (Govern/Map/Measure/Manage) AI risk management MITRE F3 (Fight Fraud Framework) v1.1 (2026-04-09) 8 tactics · 123 techniques · 94 fraud-relevant skills Cyber-enabled financial fraud TTPs Example — each skill maps only to the frameworks relevant to it (one may hit all six, another just a couple): Skill ATT&CK NIST CSF ATLAS D3FEND AI RMF F3 analyzing-network-traffic-of-malware T1071 DE.CM AML.T0047 D3-NTA MEASURE-2.6 — detecting-business-email-compromise T1566 DE.AE — — — F1005.006 · monetization 🆕 MITRE Fight Fraud Framework (F3) — 94 fraud-relevant skills The MITRE Fight Fraud Framework (F3) was released April 9, 2026 by MITRE's Center for Threat-Informed Defense (CTID), co-developed with JPMorganChase, Citigroup, Lloyds Banking Group, Standard Chartered, CrowdStrike, Verizon Business, FS-ISAC, and others. It is an ATT&CK-compatible TTP catalog for cyber-enabled financial fraud — filling the gap ATT&CK leaves after initial compromise. F3 v1.1 adds two fraud-specific tactics that ATT&CK does not enumerate: Positioning ( FA0001 ) — actions taken after access to collect/manipulate data and prepare the fraud (synthetic-identity seeding, account warming, beneficiary setup, SIM-swap pre-positioning, banking-session hijack). Monetization ( FA0002 ) — converting stolen assets into usable funds (money-mule layering, APP fraud, crypto off-ramping, card cash-out, refund/chargeback abuse). Fraud-specific techniques use F1XXX IDs (e.g. F1005.003 Add Beneficiary, F1025.003 Wire Transfer, F1007 Adversary-in-the-Browser); reused ATT&CK techniques keep their T1XXX IDs. Mappings live in each skill's mitre_f3: frontmatter block — all 123 F3 v1.1 technique IDs were verified against the upstream STIX bundle. See docs/mitre-f3-mapping.md for the schema. MITRE ATT&CK v19.1 — 805/817 skills mapped Every skill carries a mitre_attack frontmatter list validated against MITRE ATT&CK v19.1 (the latest release) using the official mitreattack-python library — 290 distinct techniques and sub-techniques (146 base + 144 sub) across Enterprise, ICS, and Mobile. Zero revoked or deprecated IDs. v19.1's restructured Defense Evasion (now split into Stealth and Defense Impairment ) is reflected below. Tactic ID Skills Reconnaissance TA0043 103 Resource Development TA0042 22 Initial Access TA0001 467 Execution TA0002 350 Persistence TA0003 444 Privilege Escalation TA0004 464 Stealth TA0005 442 Defense Impairment TA0112 92 Credential Access TA0006 202 Discovery TA0007 237 Lateral Movement TA0008 68 Collection TA0009 172 Command and Control TA0011 123 Exfiltration TA0010 82 Impact TA0040 50 Quick start # Option 1: npx (recommended) npx skills add mukul975/Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills # Option 2: Git clone git clone https://github.com/mukul975/Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills.git cd Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills Works immediately with Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and any agentskills.io -compatible platform. 🌍 GARS-2026 — Global Agentic AI Readiness Survey I'm running a global academic study measuring how ready security professionals,
developers, and enterprise teams actually are for agentic AI — MCP servers,
tool calling, governance, and human-in-the-loop workflows. If you use this repo, your response would be a genuinely valuable data point. 📋 Take the survey (10 min): Survey Link 60 questions · Anonymous · Supervised by SRH Berlin You get 50 Casky Tokens for early access to casky.ai Results published open access under CC-BY 4.0 🚀 Try it on the Playground Experience Casky.ai hands-on — no setup required. → Launch Playground on Casky.ai The playground lets you: Run live cybersecurity skill exercises against real targets See AI agents execute structured skills in real time Explore MITRE ATT&CK mapped workflows interactively Test threat hunting, DFIR, and penetration testing scenarios No installation. No configuration. Just open and start. Why this exists The cybersecurity workforce gap hit 4.8 million unfilled roles globally in 2024 (ISC2). AI agents can help close that gap — but only if they have structured domain knowledge to work from. Today's agents can write code and search the web, but they lack the practitioner playbooks that turn a generic LLM into a capable security analyst. Existing security tool repos give you wordlists, payloads, or exploit code. None of them give an AI agent the structured decision-making workflow a senior analyst follows: when to use each technique, what prerequisites to check, how to execute step-by-step, and how to verify results. That is the gap this project fills. Anthropic Cybersecurity Skills is not a collection of scripts or checklists. It is an AI-native knowledge base built from the ground up for the agentskills.io standard  — YAML frontmatter for sub-second discovery, structured Markdown for step-by-step execution, and reference files for deep technical context.  Every skill encodes real practitioner workflows, not generated summaries.

github.abstract: Agent Sprite Forge Languages: English | 繁體中文 | 簡體中文 | 日本語 | 한국어 0.4 launch teaser: every frame is real ASF output. One still → a whole game-ready sprite set Approve one generated still. Get every action of the character, keyed, looped, timed and exported for your engine. Agent skills for Claude Code (plugin), Codex and Grok . The agent generates a master still with the best image route you have, makes one image-to-video clip per action from it, and deterministic Python tools gate, key, register, loop, retime, finish and package every action for Godot, Aseprite or a web game. 1. One approved master still Generated by the local Codex CLI ( image_gen ), take 1 of 3. 2. Six actions, one image-to-video clip each Grok image-to-video (local CLI), soft-matte keyed, registered, loops picked by measurement, one-shots retimed to game speed, HD finish with the colour lock. Real timing. 3. In a scene: the packaged run, attack and idle over a generated background. The run speed is measured from the contact foot, so the feet do not slide. Every frame comes from the 2026-10-06 live run; nothing is mocked up. Pixel looks · Hibit style · What's new · Quickstart · Routes and providers · Pipeline · Maps · Showcase · Tools New: pixel looks, 1x sprites that follow a reference A whole fight from pixel-look sprites, rendered at 1x and shown at 2x: four 1x characters (masters of 33x55 to 87x86) and 14 sets with 168 drawings read back from image-to-video clips. The plate behind them is a generated painting brought down to 384x216 and 40 colours. The white hit flashes and the knight's fade are the demo's; nothing else is added. An image model asked for pixel art paints a picture of pixels: blocks of uneven size (15 to 30 px in the picture below), 88,410 colours in one small figure, soft edges. Shrinking it does not help: resized plainly to the sprite's size it still has 1,033 colours. Hibit gets round this by never asking for pixel art. Pixel looks go the other way, for the classic small sprite that follows a look you like: the look is never described in words, one sprite you like is the reference for the whole cast, and the picture the model paints is read back onto a real grid. pixel_look.py master finds the picture's own grid, takes one flat colour from every block, keeps the figure's proportions, brings the colours down to a palette and closes the outline by rule. What comes out can be counted: 33x55 pixels, 48 colours, alpha 0 or 255, a 2.5 KB PNG. What the image model painted 1254x1254 px. The figure alone has 88,410 colours and its blocks are 15 to 30 px: no grid fits it. Resized plainly to 33x55 Nearest sampling, shown at 7x: 1,033 colours, the ground's green left in 3 cells. Bilinear gives 1,275 colours and 413 soft pixels. pixel_look.py master The same picture read on its own grid, shown at 7x: 33x55, 48 colours, no soft pixel. The same part of the face: the picture at 2x (left) and the sprite at 40x (right). The cast follows the first sprite. Every further character is drawn beside the first sprite in one picture ( ask-cast , cast ), so it keeps the pixel size and stands as tall: a mage, a skeleton knight and a frost dragon, 48 colours each. Poses, views and motion from the master. A pose is the master reproduced with one change (the sword pose: 217 cells changed, 91% of the master kept); a view is drawn beside the master. Motion comes from an image-to-video clip of that sprite: pixel_motion.py reads every frame back on the sprite's lattice and palette (the attack: 21 drawings picked from 145 video frames). The number is the drawings of each set. Measured on the run (2026-11-12) The swordsman's generated picture (the figure) 1254x1254, 88,410 colours, blocks 15-30 px The same picture resized to 33x55: nearest / bilinear 1,033 colours / 1,275 colours and 413 soft pixels pixel_look.py master 33x55, 48 colours, 0 soft pixels, 2.5 KB The cast: mage / skeleton knight / frost dragon 45x56 / 50x55 / 87x86, 48 colours each The sword pose from the master 217 cells changed, 91% of the master kept The attack set from one clip 21 drawings from 145 video frames The fight 14 sets, 168 drawings; every drawing has only its sprite's own colours and no soft pixel What's new: pixel_look.py (generate2dsprite): ask-master and master draw the figure you like again, alone and large, and read it as the 1x master; ask-cast and cast draw every further character beside the master; ask-pose , pose , ask-view and view make poses and side or back views from the master; lineup puts everything on one ground line and reports the heights. pixel_motion.py (video2dsprite): prepare , frames , finish , measure , breath : the frames of an image-to-video clip read back on the sprite's lattice and palette, a loop or an action picked from them, and an animation.json 3.0 package with nearest sampling. Only on request. Nothing else changes: the HD, pixel and hibit finishes and their defaults are untouched. The reference sets the look (pixel size, shading, outline); the characters are your own. The whole route, what you accept and when, and its limits: references/pixel-looks.md . New: hibit, real pixel art from flat AI art Pip's Star Grove, a one-screen demo built only from hibit output: autopilot gameplay captured from the game canvas (480x270, shown at 2x). FX: pixelfx by Patch (MIT). Never ask an image model for "pixel art": it paints fake, uneven pixels. The hibit style asks it for clean flat lineless art (at most 3 tones per material, no outlines) and makes the pixels afterwards: one palette per character learned from the source pixels, an 8x8 majority-vote downscale (every pixel is the palette colour that covered most of its cell, never a blend), hysteresis against flicker, eyes and glints kept, binary alpha, and a 1 px outline whose colour comes from the sprite itself. Flat art in, pixel art out The approved master (Codex) and the hibit finish of the idle at 80 px: 16 colours learned from the source plus the outline colour, which --outline auto takes from the sprite's dominant hue (#380500, a deep red-brown from the orange fur). Never a fixed orange. Whole sets, one palette per character Pip (idle, walk, cast, hurt) and a magma slime (idle, crawl, attack): Grok image-to-video clips through sprite_set.py --finish hibit , 12 fps. Every action reuses the first action's palette and outline. FX: pixelfx (recommended) or the image route For hibit effects we recommend pixelfx by Patch: a library of code-driven pixel-art effects (fire, arcane, impacts, weather, pickups, UI) that fits the style and renders for free on your machine. It is a separate MIT project: clone it yourself ( git clone https://github.com/patch-gg/pixelfx , Node 18+) and the skill finds it. fx_pixelfx.py check picks the route; a route you name wins. A: pixelfx installed (recommended) B: image route (always available) Frames per effect 16-91 at 30 fps 4 (one 2x2 sheet) Cost free (local Node) one generated image per effect Look pixelfx's own style, recoloured with --ramp and --snap your game's flat style and palette Credit every render ships CREDITS.txt (pixelfx's MIT license and notice) the image route, like every sprite A: pixelfx arcane/star-fall recoloured to Pip's palette, impacts/hit-spark , spawn/poof , spawn/coin-drop . B: image route Codex 2x2 FX sheets, keyed and registered by process , made pixel art by the hibit_fx.py step (Pip's palette for the stars and coins, 6 learned colours for the spark and the poof). Full 50 s of autopilot play, same seed: with pixelfx FX (MP4) · with image-route FX (MP4) .

🦜 VieNeu-TTS VieNeu-TTS is the next generation of on-device Vietnamese TTS: 10,000+ hours of bilingual training, instant voice cloning , a dedicated Podcast/Conversation mode, and extremely fast — real-time streaming with first audio in ~115 ms, RTF ≈ 0.01–0.02 batched on a consumer GPU (RTX 3060), ~2× real-time on a plain CPU ( benchmarks ). Important 🦜 VieNeu-TTS v4 — available on vieneu.io VieNeu-TTS v4 delivers near-original voice cloning fidelity , allowing a short reference clip to be reproduced with very high speaker similarity. Due to the strength of its voice-cloning capabilities and the potential for misuse, v4 is proprietary and will not be open-sourced . It is available exclusively through the VieNeu API / vieneu.io . VieNeu-TTS v3 Turbo remains the latest open-source version available in this repository. Future open-source releases, including potential v3.x updates, may also be published here. Natural reading style everywhere — the style follows the reference voice (the style argument is deprecated and ignored). Emotion / non-verbal cues (experimental) : drop [cười] , [thở dài] , [hắng giọng] straight into the text. Batched generation (batch size up to 32), including a multi-speaker Conversation mode that batches the whole script regardless of speaker. Instant voice cloning from a 3–8s clip, with automatic reference denoising. Real-time streaming + OpenAI-compatible API + Docker — POST /v1/audio/speech drop-in for the OpenAI SDK / Pipecat / LiveKit; first audio in ~115 ms and 16 concurrent streams under 200 ms on a single RTX 3060 (32 max), CPU-only streaming too. others.title: Characterizing and Detecting Bugs at the Interfaces of OpenBSD Privilege-Separated Programs
others.abstract: Compartmentalization is an approach that limits the amount of damage a bug or security breach can wreak by decomposing a program into isolated compartments that each run with the least degree of privilege necessary. When compartmentalizing a program, developers must carefully harden the communications between compartments (i.e., compartment interfaces) to prevent attacks from spreading across boundaries. Unfortunately, this hardening is error-prone and often ad-hoc, leading to Compartment Interface Vulnerabilities (CIVs), a class of bugs that can render compartmentalized programs no more secure than their monolithic counterparts. Despite the potential impact of these bugs, the community has little understanding of how effective today's interface defenses are. This work systematically evaluates the strengths and limitations of CIV defenses deployed in production-grade compartmentalized programs. We audit a representative corpus of 25 popular compartmentalized programs in OpenBSD using a combination of manual analysis, fuzzing, and LLM agents. Our study identifies 81 CIVs, some over a decade old, with impacts as varied as memory corruption, information leakage, and logic bugs, and as severe as arbitrary code execution. We systematize our findings to extract high-level patterns that characterize these issues and derive more effective approaches to address them. Our results expose the strengths of OpenBSD's approach, such as how its avoidance of shared memory eliminates entire classes of issues. However, we also show that even programs compartmentalized by security experts remain vulnerable to recurring, high-impact CIV patterns. At the core, these findings highlight the need for clear (and ideally formal) specifications of compartment interfaces to achieve systematic counter-measures. This paper demonstrates flaws in existing compartmentalization schemes and provides a foundation for future work on the discovery and mitigation of CIVs.

others.title: LEASH: Zero-Trust Containment for AI Agent Swarms
others.abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly spawn sub-agent swarms that carry derived credentials to APIs, databases, and production infrastructure. When an operator kills a misbehaving orchestrator, its descendants keep exercising valid credentials for minutes to hours, since every deployed revocation mechanism needs network connectivity to a central authority, unavailable precisely when the network is degraded or adversarial. This paper presents LEASH - Liveness-Enforced Authorization for Swarm Hierarchies, which applies the zero-trust principle of continuous verification to a delegation hierarchy without a reachable authority. A parent emits a signed, epoch-indexed liveness beacon every Δh seconds, where Δh is the beacon interval, and each child staples a fresh beacon into every authentication proof, and the enforcement point checks freshness using only cached public keys and a local clock. Revocation happens by omission: when beacons stop, all descendants fail closed within a bounded zombie window Wz ≤ Wmax  + Δh + ϵ , where Wmax  is the maximum beacon age and ϵ is the clock skew. Immediate-parent verification at O(1) and full-chain verification at O(d), where d is the hierarchy depth, extend this bound against compromised intermediates. We evaluate LEASH with real GPT-4o-mini agent swarms: 0.71% tool-call overhead, cascading revocation across a 49-agent four-level hierarchy within bound, and 295 × less credential-theft exposure versus OAuth 2.0. Under prompt injection that bypasses application-layer guardrails, LEASH denies every post-revocation tool call, since enforcement sits below the LLM.

others.title: SymSan: Mitigating Malware Embedding in Large Language Models via Parameter Space Symmetry
others.abstract: Despite the considerable advantages of open-source large language models (LLMs) in terms of interpretability and customizability, the full-access sharing paradigm inevitably exposes them to a severe security threat, i.e., malware embedding attacks (MEAs), where adversaries embed malware binaries (i.e., payloads) into model parameters for subsequent execution. While existing sanitization defenses have been explored to eliminate payloads within parameters, they exhibit limited generalization against emerging MEAs and lack theoretical guarantees for model utility preservation. In this paper, we propose SymSan, an effective LLM sanitization method grounded in parameter space symmetry theory. SymSan leverages rigorously designed permutation and scaling symmetries, systematically transforming parameter matrices across complementary component pairs, thereby eliminating embedded payloads while ensuring mathematical functional equivalence. Experiments across diverse LLMs against a wide spectrum of MEAs demonstrate that SymSan achieves at least 0.47 BER against all evaluated existing MEAs while maintaining equivalent model performance on both foundational and downstream tasks, significantly outperforming all baselines.

others.title: Improving Transparency and Accountability in AI Data Use
others.abstract: The rise of generative AI has rapidly increased the amount of data needed to both train models and ground generated responses with updated factual information. These needs are particularly relevant to AI-based chatbots. Developers of such systems initially gather training data to teach models how to generate new content, then provide deployed models with tools to reference information online (''real-time content retrieval'') to ensure content generated is up to date. However, implementation details of this data acquisition often remain unknown. This dissertation seeks to understand how AI models - specifically proprietary AI chatbots - ingest and process content from the web. The long-term goal of this research is to increase the control people have over how their online content is used in AI models. Our research will do this by unveiling details of existing data use methodologies in AI systems and creating new tools to control such data use. Thus far our research has revealed that AI chatbots acquire data from websites in unexpected ways, spoofing as human visitors or scraping data from third parties. Future work will perform additional measurement studies of generative AI systems and develop new tools to give web hosts greater control over their data.

others.title: Time Will Tell: Illuminating Causes of Score Inflation in Source Code Vulnerability Detection Benchmarks
others.abstract: LLM-based source code vulnerability detection (SCVD) reports strong benchmark performance that does not hold up in the real world. Use of random splitting in test-set construction has been widely blamed for permitting time-travel and inter-commit leakage, but neither mechanism has been empirically isolated. We evaluate five different cross-validation strategies across eight fine-tuned and eight zero-shot LLMs on MegaVul-C; every strategy is also evaluated on the same held-out future set to separate training-set from test-set effects. Random splitting inflates reported test-set F1 by ∼ 34% for fine-tuned models and ∼ 16% for zero-shot models. On the shared holdout set, models fine-tuned using random and temporal training splits achieve statistically equivalent performance within ± 2 pp (pTOST < 0.001), which places the inflation on test-set construction. Matched comparisons that isolate inter-commit leakage and time-travel are equivalent on the holdout set within the same margin. Correcting the train-test CWE distribution by resampling, our proxy for evolving vulnerability patterns, does not close the gap either. The gap instead reflects differences between the training and evaluation distributions, which we localize but do not reduce to a single causal property. Temporal splitting remains necessary for realistic evaluation because it reduces the optimistic bias of random test-set construction. We recommend Temporal LOO Block CV, which preserves the variance reduction of K-fold evaluation while inducing distribution shift at each fold boundary. All split-generation, analysis, and training code is released to support reproducible evaluation of LLMs for SCVD.

others.title: Governing AI Agent with Capability and Delegation Chain
others.abstract: As LLM-based agents move from personal productivity assistants to enterprise workflow executors, security requirements shift from controlling model outputs to governing real-world decisions and tool invocations. Existing defenses improve robustness, but still struggle to enforce fine-grained, verifiable authority continuously across multi-hop delegation in autonomous workflows. We present CapAgent, an access-control and identity-delegation framework for AI agents that combines capability-constrained credentials with delegation-chain semantics. In CapAgent, authority is encoded as cryptographically protected, derivable credentials with explicit API/parameter constraints, lifecycle rules, and cross-hop provenance. CapAgent couples a protocol for issuance, derivation, verification, and auditing with a three-layer architecture, and we implement it as a layered SDK with CLI and MCP integration, together with a multi-agent governance prototype for intent compilation. Our evaluation includes symbolic verification, enforcement case studies of out-of-scope actions, public agent-security benchmarks (ASB and AgentDojo), and performance measurements of core operations. Results indicate that CapAgent achieves least-privilege multi-hop delegation with practical near-local overhead, supporting production-grade autonomous agent operations.

others.title: Out of Tune: How Different Fine-Tuning Methods Affect Information Security
others.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) enables task specialization but introduces privacy risks through training data memorization. Practitioners deploying fine-tuned LLMs in sensitive domains such as medicine, law, and finance must choose among fine-tuning methods without clear guidance on the privacy implications of that choice. We compare full fine-tuning, partial fine-tuning, and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by measuring how much sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) each method leaks from training data, using planted canaries to track memorization. Six Llama configurations (3B and 8B parameters) are evaluated across the medical, legal, and finance domains under three extraction attack types: prefix attacks, random prompting, and completion attacks. Full fine-tuning leaks the most on average, followed by LoRA. Partial fine-tuning leaks the least in every configuration we tested, though the relative ordering of full fine-tuning and LoRA varies. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, LoRA's parameter efficiency does not yield the strongest privacy protection; we attribute this to LoRA's architectural breadth across all transformer layers. The performance-privacy trade-off these findings expose has direct consequences for deployment. Even partial fine-tuning on the 3B model, our best configuration, leaked canaries, so practitioners should assume some leakage by default.

others.title: Emergence-Driven Security of LLM Agents
others.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer limited to text generators, but they can also plan, call tools, delegate tasks to other agents, act within external environments, and change states in response to their actions. In Anthropic’s recent report on an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign involving Claude Code, individual subtasks appeared legitimate when evaluated in isolation but became malicious when combined into an autonomous attack sequence. Consequently, the security of such complex LLM-based agentic systems may fail even when each component appears secure in isolation. This position and open-problem paper argues that LLM agent security should be studied as emergence-driven security: the analysis of security properties that arise from the interactions among agents and its components over time. We define emergence-driven security and provide a conceptual taxonomy to classify emergent security-related phenomena in LLM agents, covering both beneficial and harmful forms of emergence. Based on these insights, we propose EASE, an Emergence-Aware Security Evaluation framework that provides a systematic process for assessing how interactions among agents combine over time to produce harmful or beneficial system-level security outcomes. Finally, we conclude by outlining open problems for studying emergent behavior in LLM agents in the context of security. The paper is intended to provide a foundation for examining how the emerging capabilities and operational needs of LLM agents may shape security evaluations that go beyond static, model-level testing.

others.title: ArchProof: A Sound Output-Contribution Certificate for Dormant-Gate Path Backdoors in ONNX Models
others.abstract: Architectural backdoors are malicious subgraphs hard-wired into a neural network's computational graph. They survive weight-based defenses and are flagged by commercial scanners as a first-class threat to ONNX deployment. Existing detection relies on heuristic signatures or probabilistic sampling; a sound deterministic quantitative certificate for any formally defined subclass of this threat is missing. We present ArchProof, a verifier that reads an ONNX model and a clean-input calibration set and returns a sound output-contribution ε-certificate over a decidable class of additive dormant-gate path backdoors. The certificate is a worst-case bound, not an estimate of what a trigger does to the output. Its use is threefold: a one-sided verdict, a per-gate ranking, and a bound that reaches zero once the flagged gates are removed. Three theorems then bound how the certificate behaves under deployment stress: it degrades within bounds when the calibration set is poisoned, a greedy algorithm finds the smallest set of gates to remove for any target level, and it stays stable across semantics-preserving ONNX exports. We evaluate on production CNN, transformer-encoder, and decoder-only LLM ONNX graphs against heuristic and ablation baselines.

others.title: SpecStega: Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography Based on Speculative Sampling in Asymmetric Resource Scenarios
others.abstract: Provably secure generative steganography embeds secret messages by guiding the sampling process of a Language Model (LM) without altering its original probability distribution. Existing methods typically rely on a strict white-box assumption, requiring both the sender and receiver to share an identical LM. To ensure the linguistic fluency necessary to avoid abnormal behavior, the shared model is usually a large LM. However, this assumption is often impractical in asymmetric resource scenarios where receivers are constrained to resource-limited edge devices (e.g., mobile phones) capable of running only a small LM. This computational discrepancy creates a covertness dilemma between achieving high-quality stego text generation and ensuring efficient decodability. While existing black-box methods attempt to bypass model access for decoding, they fail to fully leverage the receiver's available resources, resulting in limited payload capacity. To resolve this dilemma, we propose a novel gray-box steganography, SpecStega, that utilizes the shared draft small LM for message embedding to ensure receiver compatibility, while leveraging speculative sampling with the target large LM to refine the output. This ensures that the final stego text aligns with the target LM's distribution, preserving high-quality linguistic fluency and security. To mitigate decoding errors caused by the distribution mismatch between the target and draft LMs, we introduce a robust decoding mechanism based on evidence accumulation and noise suppression. Experimental results demonstrate that SpecStega increases payload capacity by over 20x compared to the existing black-box solution in asymmetric resource scenarios. Our method successfully bridges a critical gap in practical steganography, achieving the high-quality stego text generated by the target LM while maintaining efficient decodability via the draft LM.

others.title: 11th Workshop on Traffic Measurements for Cybersecurity (WTMC)
others.abstract: The Workshop on Traffic Measurements for Cybersecurity (WTMC) provides a forum for research grounded in traffic measurements and empirical observations of security-relevant online phenomena. WTMC brings together researchers and practitioners from academia and industry to examine how measurements of network traffic, protocols, applications, platforms, and Internet-scale infrastructure can improve our understanding of cyberattacks, online abuse, defensive mechanisms, and their operational impact. The workshop welcomes original research, measurement methodologies, empirical studies, operational experience, and reappraisals of previous findings. Its scope includes malware, botnets, phishing, network anomalies, abuse infrastructures, attack detection and mitigation, the economics of cybersecurity, and the emerging role of generative AI in cyberattacks and defense.

others.title: Embodied AI Must Treat Visual Bias as a Safety Primitive, Not a Robustness Penalty
others.abstract: While embodied agents increasingly incorporate diverse sensors, they predominantly rely on learned visual representations for manipulation and control. However, when visual preferences are tightly coupled with action generation, benign cues can induce task failures, unsafe motions, or exploitable vulnerabilities. We present a diagnostic study of visual bias as a safety primitive for embodied AI evaluation and defense: an independently operationalizable property tied to an identifiable risk class, not a standalone safety guarantee. Agents should be assessed not merely on task success, but also on whether their actions remain grounded in visual evidence relevant to the task. We study this risk through controlled visual variations under task-equivalent conditions, naturalistic distractors aligned with inherited visual preferences, and counterfactual action analysis. Our results show that benign perceptual changes can produce divergent behavior, while task-irrelevant content can receive disproportionate action relevance and induce physical failures. We further introduce a counterfactual detection method that combines persistent region selection with changes in predicted actions after masking, helping distinguish behaviorally relevant preference-aligned content from regions that are merely visually salient. These findings provide preliminary diagnostic evidence of visual bias and demonstrate the need for broader preference discovery, visual shortcut mining, and failure mode search to improve predeployment risk coverage and guide targeted mitigation in both model development and real-world deployment.

others.title: Code-SeC: A Decoding-time Probing Method for Characterizing Secret Memorization in Code LLM
others.abstract: Code Large Language Models (Code LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in code generation and completion. While these models are known to memorize portions of their training data, existing approaches to evaluate credential memorization rely on output-level inspection or adversarial prompt crafting, leaving the internal decoding behaviors that underlie secret leakage unexplored. In this paper, we conduct a token-level investigation of hard-coded credential memorization in Code LLMs during routine code completion. We report two findings: (1) traces of memorized secrets persist in the token candidate space, indicating that standard output-level evaluation underestimates the true extent of memorization; (2) the generation of real secrets exhibits statistically distinct uncertainty dynamics compared to hallucinated strings, providing a reliable intrinsic signal for memorization detection. Based on these findings, we propose Code-SeC (Code Secret Characterization), a decoding-time diagnostic framework that monitors uncertainty signals along the decoding trajectory and performs targeted distribution adjustments to uncover latent credential memorization. Experimental results show that Code-SeC effectively detects memorized code secrets across representative Code LLMs and secret types, providing comprehensive empirical evidence that hard-coded credential memorization is prevalent in current code completion models.

others.title: Reverse Prompt Engineering in Generative AI: A Baseline for Deepfake, Deception and Disinformation Mitigation
others.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has democratised content creation while scaling systemic threats in Deepfakes, Deception, and Disinformation (D3). As traditional content detection and watermarking are increasingly bypassed, this paper presents a position and baseline synthesis of Reverse Prompt Engineering (RPE) as a defensive capability. RPE inverts the generative pipeline to infer plausible instruction prompts and support, rather than definitively proving source-model attribution. Grounded in threat telemetry, we synthesise representative RPE frameworks while explicitly delineating the evidentiary limits of prompt recovery, attribution, and content provenance. We further evaluate RPE across public information, legal, and policy/governance viewpoints, analyse key technical limitations such as cross-modal generalisation, and outline a research roadmap to establish RPE as a cornerstone of digital provenance and AI accountability.

others.title: Does AI Amplify Online Hate- A Multi-Modal Measurement Study on 4chan's /pol/
others.abstract: As generative AI models gain widespread adoption, an urgent question arises: are they being exploited to produce hateful content in online communities? We present the first large-scale, multi-modal measurement study to investigate this question, drawing on 465M text posts spanning 2016-2026 and 16.9M images spanning 2021-2025 from 4chan's /pol/ board. Specifically, we focused on two hate targets with long-established phenomena in parallel: anti-Indian hate and anti-Semitic hate. By benchmarking five text and five image AI detectors on hateful content, we deploy the best-performing detectors on over 31K long-form hateful posts and approximately 50K hateful images to measure AI-generated content prevalence. We find that the two targets exhibit different growth patterns: anti-Indian hate is substantially self-sustaining, with 46.15% of detected peaks driven by organized community campaigns rather than external events, against only 5.88% for anti-Semitic hate, which is instead largely reactive, with 94.12% of peaks triggered by real-world events such as the October 7 Hamas attack. AI-generated hateful posts have grown steadily since late 2022, reaching 1.42% of long-form posts by 2025. More importantly, AI adoption diverges across the two targets. For anti-Indian hate, AI content prevalence correlates significantly with slur frequency, nearly doubles during hate peaks, and AI-generated posts are 55.72% more toxic than human-written ones. Anti-Semitic hate, by contrast, shows no significant AI-hate correlation, indicating that AI tools are more widely adopted in campaign-driven hate than in established hate discourse. Lead-lag analysis reveals that hate campaigns precede AI adoption by approximately three months, suggesting that generative AI serves as an accelerator for existing hate movements rather than an independent driver.

others.title: Secrecy in Squirrel and the Post-Compromise Security of a Ratchet
others.abstract: Ratchets are critical cryptographic protocols deployed in many secure messaging applications such as Signal Messenger, WhatsApp, and Apple's iMessage PQ3, which aim for strong guarantees such as Post-Compromise Security (PCS). Computer-aided cryptography can be used to increase confidence in security protocols but, until now, has been unable to prove PCS in the computational model for a ratchet due to the complexity of the cryptographic arguments involved. Existing mechanized PCS analyses have been limited to the symbolic model. We tackle this problem with Squirrel, which is well-suited to study such stateful protocols. The task is still a challenge, due to the intricate reasoning required, and because Squirrel's indirect modeling of secrecy has difficulties in scaling to such a complex proof. To address these issues, we develop a novel logical framework in Squirrel that allows to reason on secrecy as a first-class notion, and we validate our approach by verifying the PCS of an asymmetric ratchet. This provides the first mechanized computational proof of PCS to date for a ratchet, and possibly for any protocol.

others.title: POSTER: UniAlert: Cost-Efficient Unified Representation of Multi-Source Heterogeneous Alert Logs with LLMs
others.abstract: Multi-zone IDS deployments improve detection coverage but also introduce large volumes of heterogeneous alerts generated by diverse IDS platforms. Existing alert denoising methods are not readily applicable to such alerts, as they typically assume a unified schema and consistent field semantics. Alert normalization approaches partially mitigate this issue by leveraging manually crafted prior knowledge. However, constructing and maintaining such knowledge requires substantial expert effort and limits their adaptability to evolving log schemas. To address these challenges, we present UniAlert, an LLM-based system for accurate and cost-efficient unified representation of alert logs. UniAlert extracts field-level context from log trees to constrain LLM reasoning and improve field mapping accuracy. It further uses incremental field-mapping templates and selectively invokes LLMs only for unseen log formats or template updates, significantly reducing token cost. Preliminary results show that, compared with state-of-the-art methods, UniAlert improves field-mapping F1 by 20.06%-57.78% while reducing token consumption by 98.69% compared with LLM-only.

others.title: Accio: Detecting Privilege Escalation Vulnerabilities in DBMSs via Minimum Privilege Set Calculation
others.abstract: Access control mechanisms in DBMSs enforce user privileges for executing SQL operations. They are critical for protecting the confidentiality and integrity of stored data. However, implementation errors can lead to privilege escalation, allowing unauthorized actions that appear legitimate to the system. We refer to such errors as privilege escalation vulnerabilities (PEVs), which can result in severe consequences, including denial of service, data leakage, and data tampering. Despite their serious impact, the characteristics of PEVs remain largely unexplored, and systematic detection methods are still lacking. In this paper, we present a motivation study of 63 real-world privilege escalation cases from 5 widely used DBMSs. Our analysis shows that many vulnerabilities stem from missing privilege checks, incorrect privilege resolution, or operation-privilege mismatches. Detecting these PEVs requires careful reasoning about the interactions between SQL operations, user privileges, and execution contexts. Guided by these insights, we design and implement Accio, which detects privilege escalation vulnerabilities via minimum privilege set calculation. It models privilege hierarchies, computes the minimum set of privileges required for each SQL command, and checks consistency against expected policies. We evaluated Accio on seven widely used DBMSs, discovering 26 previously unknown PEVs, all confirmed, and 23 of which have been fixed. Accio also successfully detects historical privilege escalation cases and has been positively recognized by developers for its practical impact.

others.title: zkTransformer: Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs for LLM Inference via Einsum Arithmetization and Structured Exponentiation Lookups
others.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed through cloud APIs; however, their inference processes are opaque and cannot be externally audited without revealing proprietary model parameters. Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) enable verifiable inference while preserving model confidentiality, but existing zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) systems remain difficult to deploy in practice due to limitations in developer usability, completeness of prover implementations, and the cost of lookup operations. We present \zkt, an end-to-end zkML framework for transformer inference that addresses these challenges while achieving high prover performance. To improve usability and correctness, we introduce \zkes, a new sumcheck-based arithmetization that lifts linear tensor operations to an AI-friendly abstraction based on Einstein summation (Einsum), enabling automatic compilation of such operations into a single Sumcheck instance without manual circuit engineering over low-level addition and multiplication gates. To reduce the cost of nonlinear operations, we further propose \zkexp, a structured lookup technique for exponentiation that eliminates the need for table-sized commitments. Together, these techniques provide a unified and model-agnostic framework for verifiable transformer inference, supporting standard architectures such as GPT-2 and LLaMA2-7B. We implement and open-source \zkt. On GPT-2, it achieves an amortized prover time of 3.4 seconds per token, representing a 5--10× speedup over state-of-the-art systems such as zkLLM and zkGPT.

others.title: Global-View Reasoning with LLMs for Real-World Vulnerability Detection
others.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in code generation and other software engineering tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world security vulnerability detection still remains limited. A key observation is that while LLMs exhibit strong semantic understanding and security analysis capabilities on code snippets, these strengths are rarely extended to large-scale real-world programs. In this work, we propose SemScan, a novel vulnerability detection approach that harnesses LLMs' local reasoning capabilities to enable global security analysis. SemScan establishes an iterative loop of evidence collection and evidence-guided semantic synthesis. Our evaluation on a Python CVE vulnerability dataset and 200 popular real-world Python projects demonstrates that SemScan significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tools, uncovering 62 previously unknown serious vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and insecure deserialization flaws. To date, 22 of these vulnerabilities have been confirmed and assigned CVE identifiers.
